core_principles.text: Incorporating a forward lean of the trunk during a forward lunge significantly increases the ankle plantar flexor moment, hip extensor moment, and activation of the gluteus maximus and biceps femoris muscles relative to a vertical trunk posture.
Restricting forward translation of the lead-limb shank (maintaining a vertical shank) may reduce patellofemoral joint stress in the front knee, but it increases the stress placed on the trail knee.
Technique recommendations for the forward lunge must consider the biomechanical demands imposed on both knees, as the trail limb generally experiences high joint stress.

common_mistakes.text: Allowing both a forward trunk lean and a forward shank position simultaneously during a lunge maximizes the patellofemoral stress in the lead limb.

specific_findings.text: In a study of 18 healthy participants, the trail limb experienced greater total patellofemoral joint stress relative to the lead limb, regardless of trunk and shank position (P<.0001).
A lunge variation with a vertical shank position resulted in significantly greater peak patellofemoral joint stress in the trail limb relative to the lead limb (P<.0001).
A forward trunk and shank position resulted in the highest patellofemoral stress in the lead limb (P<.0001).
The head, arms, and trunk consist of approximately 55% of body mass, which explains why trunk position has a significant influence on lower extremity joint moments during the lunge.

consequences.text: Leaning the trunk forward during a lunge increases the load and patellofemoral joint stress on the lead limb's knee when combined with a forward shank position.
Restricting forward knee travel on the lead leg shifts the physical demands, resulting in increased patellofemoral joint stress in the trail limb's knee.

core_principles.text: When performing a lunge, the spine should be kept in a neutral position to maintain natural lumbar lordosis.
To achieve proper depth during a lunge, descend until the trail knee is just prior to touching the ground.
Maintaining a neutral ankle angle helps keep the shank perpendicular to the ground, preventing anterior translation of the lead-limb knee joint center over the ankle joint center.

specific_findings.text: The study evaluated 18 healthy, recreationally active participants consisting of 5 females and 13 males, with a mean age of 34 ± 13 years, weight of 75.9 ± 10.7 kg, and height of 176.4 ± 8.9 cm.
Stride length for participants was normalized to limb length, resulting in a mean stride length of 84.4 ± 5.6 cm.
Participants were instructed to land within a target area ranging from 75% to 100% of their limb length.
Lunges were temporally regulated using a metronome set at 55 beats per minute, with each repetition lasting approximately 2 seconds for the forward phase.
In split squats, constraining the lead shank to a vertical position increases the trail-limb knee extensor moment because the trail limb must support a greater percentage of the total body weight.

consequences.text: Overuse from high frequency or magnitude of load and stress at the patellofemoral joint is implicated in the development of patellofemoral pain.
Varying the stride length during a forward lunge significantly influences the loading of the cruciate ligaments, hamstrings, and quadriceps of the lead limb.
Restricting the anterior displacement of the lead knee during a split squat increases the load and extensor moment on the trail-limb knee.

core_principles.text: Altering trunk and shank alignment during a lunge redistributes patellofemoral joint reaction forces and knee extensor impulses between the lead and trail limbs.

specific_findings.text: In a study of 18 participants, a lunge performed with a forward trunk and forward shank (FF) resulted in a lead limb peak patellofemoral joint reaction force of 42.5 ± 8.0 N·kg–1, compared to 40.7 ± 10.0 N·kg–1 for a vertical trunk and vertical shank (VV) lunge.

A lunge performed with a vertical trunk and vertical shank (VV) resulted in a significantly higher peak patellofemoral joint reaction force in the trail limb (50.7 ± 8.1 N·kg–1) compared to a forward trunk and forward shank (FF) lunge (32.6 ± 10.4 N·kg–1).

The trail limb experienced a higher knee extensor impulse during a vertical trunk, vertical shank (VV) lunge (2.8 ± 0.5 Nm·s·kg–1) compared to a forward trunk, forward shank (FF) lunge (1.9 ± 0.6 Nm·s·kg–1).

In the lead limb, a forward trunk with a vertical shank (FV) lunge produced a lower peak patellofemoral joint reaction force (35.4 ± 7.5 N·kg–1) compared to both FF (42.5 ± 8.0 N·kg–1) and VV (40.7 ± 10.0 N·kg–1) lunges.

The trail limb patellofemoral joint stress maximum was highest in the vertical trunk, vertical shank (VV) lunge (0.125 ± 0.02 MPa·kg–1) and lowest in the forward trunk, forward shank (FF) lunge (0.0940 ± 0.03 MPa·kg–1).

core_principles.text: Performing a lunge with a forward trunk and a vertical shank (FV) minimizes peak patellofemoral joint stress in the lead limb compared to a forward trunk with a forward shank (FF) or a vertical trunk with a vertical shank (VV).

A lunge performed with a vertical trunk and vertical shank (VV) or forward trunk and vertical shank (FV) results in greater peak patellofemoral joint stress in the trail limb compared to the lead limb.

specific_findings.text: The peak knee flexion angle on the lead limb averaged 90° in the vertical shank positions (FV and VV) and approximately 100° during the shank-forward position (FF).
The trail limb peak knee flexion angle averaged approximately 100° in both vertical-shank conditions (FV and VV) and approximately 105° during the shank-forward condition (FF).

Peak patellofemoral joint stress was significantly greater in the trail limb compared to the lead limb during FV and VV variations (P < .0001), but was not significantly different during FF (P = .95).
Lead-limb knee extensor impulse was significantly greater during FF relative to VV (P = .0005).
In the trail limb, the greatest patellofemoral joint reaction force occurred during the vertical trunk with vertical shank (VV) condition.

consequences.text: Allowing the lead-limb shank to migrate forward (FF) increases peak patellofemoral joint reaction force and stress in the lead limb compared to keeping a vertical shank (FV).
Maintaining an upright vertical trunk (VV) increases peak patellofemoral joint stress and reaction force in the trail limb compared to leaning the trunk forward (FF or FV).

core_principles.text: Lunge technique, including shank angle and trunk position, significantly influences both joint moments and patellofemoral kinetics of both the lead and trail limbs.
Biomechanical evaluations and recommendations for the forward lunge should consider the loading and kinematics of both the lead and trail limbs, rather than focusing solely on the lead limb.
The initial weight-acceptance phase of the lead limb involves eccentric loading of the knee extensor muscles, which is followed by concentric loading during the propulsive phase.
The position of the lead-limb shank influences how load is distributed between the lead and trail limbs during the lunge.

specific_findings.text: Patellofemoral joint stress impulse was greater in the trail limb compared to the lead limb during the forward trunk/vertical shank (FV) (P < .0001), vertical trunk/vertical shank (VV) (P < .0001), and forward trunk/forward shank (FF) (P = .0090) conditions.

In the trail limb, the patellofemoral joint stress impulse in the forward trunk/forward shank (FF) posture was significantly less than both the forward trunk/vertical shank (FV) (P = .0001) and vertical trunk/vertical shank (VV) (P < .0001) postures.
When the shank was forward, lead-limb knee extensor moments were greater relative to both vertical-shank conditions.
The lowest knee extensor moments in the trail limb occurred when the lead shank was forward.

A forward trunk and forward shank (FF) posture resulted in an approximately 15% increase in vertical ground reaction force for the lead limb and an approximately 30% decrease for the trail limb relative to the forward trunk and vertical shank (FV) posture.
Forward lean of the trunk during the forward lunge results in greater recruitment of the hamstrings.

consequences.text: Allowing the lead shank to project forward increases the knee extensor moments on the lead limb relative to keeping a vertical shank.

The trail limb experiences greater patellofemoral joint stress impulse than the lead limb across forward trunk/vertical shank, vertical trunk/vertical shank, and forward trunk/forward shank variations.

core_principles.text: Working through a limited range of motion of less than 60 degrees of knee flexion can be used to reduce peak patellofemoral joint reaction force in the lead limb during a forward lunge.
Leaning the trunk forward during a lunge increases the joint moments of the ankle plantar flexors and hip extensors.
Maintaining a vertical shank reduces peak patellofemoral joint reaction force and stress on the lead limb, but increases patellofemoral joint loading on the trail limb.

common_mistakes.text: Leaning the trunk forward shifts the muscular demand, increasing the load on the ankle plantar flexors and hip extensors.

specific_findings.text: Working through a limited range of motion of less than 60 degrees of knee flexion reduces peak patellofemoral joint reaction force in the lead limb.
Maintaining a vertical shank increases trail-limb patellofemoral joint loading to approximately 44-51 N·kg-1, which is higher than the lead-limb peak loading of 35-42 N·kg-1.
The trail limb supports body weight for a longer duration of approximately 3.5 seconds compared to approximately 2.0 seconds for the lead limb across all lunge techniques.
Patellofemoral joint stress magnitudes in lunges are approximately 7-9 MPa, which is consistent with forward-shank (7 MPa) and vertical-shank (5 MPa) lunges.
Experimental data and computer simulations suggest minimal loading of the anterior cruciate ligament during the forward lunge exercise.

consequences.text: Leaning the trunk forward increases the mechanical demand and joint moments on the ankle plantar flexors and hip extensors.
Maintaining a vertical shank to protect the lead knee shifts the load, resulting in increased patellofemoral joint reaction force and stress on the trail limb.

core_principles.text: Lunges can be executed using different variations of trunk and shank alignment, including a forward trunk with a forward shank, a forward trunk with a vertical shank, and a vertical trunk with a vertical shank.

specific_findings.text: During a forward lunge, a forward trunk lean results in a biceps femoris activation of 17.9% maximum voluntary contraction (MVC) compared to 11.9% MVC with an upright trunk.
During a forward lunge, a forward trunk lean results in a gluteus maximus activation of 22.3% maximum voluntary contraction (MVC) compared to 18.5% MVC with an upright trunk.

During a forward lunge, vastus lateralis activation is 50.9% maximum voluntary contraction (MVC) with a forward trunk lean compared to 45.6% MVC with an upright trunk, representing no significant difference.
A 54% difference in patellofemoral joint stress was demonstrated in bilateral barbell squat models when comparing those considering solely net joint moment to those including static optimization.

core_principles.text: The prescription of the forward lunge in an exercise or rehabilitative setting should consider the stresses imposed on both the lead and trail knees.

specific_findings.text: Patellofemoral joint stresses in the trail limb were greater than those in the lead limb during many of the forward lunge postures under investigation.
Peak patellofemoral joint stresses in the trail knee occurred when the trunk and lead shank were both vertical.

consequences.text: A vertical trunk and shank position will result in significant stress at the patellofemoral joint in the trail limb.
Changing trunk and shank position significantly alters joint moments and patellofemoral joint reaction force and stress in each limb.
